candidates.title: Omics Approaches: Investigating Soil Microbial Diversity and Plant-Microbe Interactions Across Diverse Ecological Communities
candidates.abstract: Soil, a fundamental component of terrestrial ecosystems, is not just a medium for plant growth but a critical element in sustaining life on Earth. It provides a wide range of ecosystem services, many of which are mediated by diverse soil processes and functions driven by soil biodiversity. Among these biological components, the soil microbiome plays a central role in regulating plant health, nutrient cycling, stress adaptation, and biomass production. Emerging research highlights the promise of both targeted and untargeted strategies for managing soil microbial communities to sustainably enhance crop yields, nutritional value, and food safety. In the context of sustainable agriculture, the intricate interactions between plants and their associated soil microbiomes are increasingly recognized as essential. Advances in high-throughput sequencing technologies, integrative omics platforms, and gene editing tools have significantly accelerated our ability to dissect these complex relationships. Omics approaches encompassing genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and beyond have revolutionized our capacity to investigate microbial diversity and the dynamic interactions between plants and microbes across diverse ecological landscapes and temporal scales. By leveraging multi-omics strategies, researchers can now construct intricate, systems-level models of plant-microbiome interactions. This not only facilitates predictions of microbial and plant responses under various environmental stressors but also unlocks promising avenues for the future of sustainable agriculture. This review provides an overview of the current state of knowledge on plant-microbe interactions, with a strong emphasis on the crucial and captivating role of established and emerging multi-omics methodologies in unraveling the complexity of soil microbial diversity and functional dynamics across ecological gradients.

candidates.title: Solitude and Delineation of Bacteria Associated with Hawked PorkMeat
candidates.abstract: This project work was carried on the solitude and delineation of pathogenic bacteria from hawked Pork meat. Pork meat were bought from the sellers and was collected in raps of aluminum foil. It was then taken to the laboratory for analysis. The sample was homogenized then pipette using 5ml sterile pipette and test tube. The dilution was then cultured on different media, MacConkey agar, Nutrient agar and blood agar then incubated at 370C for 24 hours. Discrete bacteria colonies were observed and each colony was gram-stained and examined microscopically. Biochemical test was carried out to confirm the particular bacteria present. Bacteria isolated were Staphylococcus aureus 32.4%, Bacillus subtilis 51.9%, and Escherichia coli 15.6%. This microorganism isolated from contaminated Pork meat are capable of causing illness. For instance, Staphylococcu aureus produce air exo-toxin and can withstand temperature of 1000C for 30 minutes, when ingested, it causes intoxication manifesting in 4 – 5 hours with acute diarrhea, vomiting and gastroenteritis lasting 6 – 8 hours.
candidates.journal: JOURNAL OF BIOLOGY AND GENETIC RESEARCH

candidates.title: Targeting RNA methylation to reset the tumor microenvironment
candidates.abstract: RNA methylation has emerged as an epitranscriptomic mechanism that mediates intercellular communication in the tumor microenvironment (TME). Modifications including m 6 A, m 5 C, m 1 A, and m 7 G are used by tumor, immune, and stromal cells through their respective writer–eraser–reader systems to regulate diverse functions, including metabolic reprogramming, immune checkpoint expression, immune cell polarization, and stromal remodeling. In cancer, this three-component network becomes globally dysregulated, resulting in an immunosuppressive microenvironment that promotes tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. Recent studies have shown that global methylation patterns are associated with TME immune infiltration, metabolism, and patient prognosis, suggesting that targeting the epitranscriptome may reverse the TME toward an immune-permissive state. This review summarizes current knowledge of RNA methylation across TME cell types, its dysregulation in cancer, and network-based therapeutic strategies for TME remodeling, providing a conceptual framework for biomarker discovery and combination therapy development.

candidates.title: Long-read sequencing: the resolution revolution in embryonic development and beyond
candidates.abstract: Early embryonic development and stem cell pluripotency are controlled by the coordinated regulation of transcriptomic diversity and dynamic epigenetic states. Short-read sequencing (SRS) has provided foundational insights into developmental regulation, but the fragmentation of nucleic acids before sequencing limits the characterization of full-length transcript dynamics, epigenetic change, and transposable element (TE) activity, which are key features of early embryogenesis. Here we review recent advances in long-read sequencing (LRS) and evaluate their impact on the study of embryonic development and embryonic stem cells (ESCs). LRS enables the interrogation of full-length transcript isoforms, alternative splicing events, poly(A) tail dynamics, DNA and RNA modifications, TE-derived chimeric RNAs, and haplotype-resolved regulatory features. It also supports measurements that lie outside RNA biology, including the direct measurement of telomere length, the detection of de novo retrotransposon insertions, and the profiling of chromatin accessibility on individual molecules. By preserving molecular continuity and regulatory information, LRS provides an integrated view of the transcriptional, epigenetic, and post-transcriptional mechanisms that coordinate pluripotency, lineage specification, and early cell fate decisions. We also discuss the technical and analytical limitations that still constrain the field and outline the directions in which it is moving, including single-cell, spatially resolved, and epitranscriptomic applications.
candidates.journal: Journal of Translational Genetics and Genomics

candidates.title: Quantifying priority effects in community assembly experiments
candidates.abstract: Abstract The history of community assembly can affect biodiversity and ecosystem functioning. This historical contingency is often driven by priority effects, whereby species interactions are influenced by the order and timing of species arrival. Experimental manipulations of the order of arrival of species have been instrumental in elucidating the causes and consequences of priority effects. Nevertheless, quantifying priority effects is challenging due to the complexity of experimental designs and the lack of consensus regarding the most appropriate comparisons and metrics for estimating the direction and magnitude of priority effects. This paper compares approaches that differ in (1) the reference scenario against which the performance of the response species is evaluated (synchronous arrival or reverse arrival), (2) the method used to standardise the interval between species introductions and the measurement of species performance (species‐specific or assembly‐specific comparison) and (3) the metric used to quantify priority effects. Using a previously published in vitro experiment that manipulated the order of arrival of four human‐associated Bifidobacterium species as an illustrative example, we show that different approaches and metrics to quantifying priority effects can yield divergent conclusions regarding the strength and, in some cases, even the direction of priority effects. This finding underscores the importance of carefully selecting and clearly reporting the approach and metric used, as each is best suited to address distinct questions related to arrival history. When designing experiments to quantify priority effects, we recommend always including a synchronous reference where all species are introduced simultaneously and grow for the same duration as the late‐arriving (response) species in the target arrival sequence. It may help to include a reference scenario in which species are introduced sequentially, with the response species having the same time to establish and develop in the target and reference arrival sequences. Although we could not use this approach in our study case, it seems well suited to isolate order of arrival effects on species performance. Additionally, we advocate using standardised mean differences and log response ratios to quantify priority effects, as these metrics offer robust estimates and facilitate quantitative synthesis across taxa and ecosystems.

candidates.title: Ebola virus-based antibody products cross-neutralize 2026 Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein.
candidates.abstract: The ongoing 2026 outbreak of Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) disease has highlighted the urgent need for therapeutic countermeasures. Whether Ebola virus (EBOV)-induced antibodies can cross-neutralize contemporary BDBVs is unclear. Here we test a diverse panel of EBOV-derived polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies, including plasma from humans after EBOV infection and horse plasma and mice serum immunized with available EBOV immunogens, against vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) pseudotypes presenting BDBV-2026 glycoprotein (GP). We find that all antibodies retain cross-neutralizing activity against BDBV-2026 glycoprotein. These findings identify existing Ebola virus-derived antibody preparations as candidates for rapid evaluation.

candidates.title: Mapping unsolved lipidomes accelerates lipid discovery in major bacterial pathogens.
candidates.abstract: Pathogenic bacteria use specialized lipids to promote virulence. Unlike genomes, the scope of lipids in many bacterial pathogens remains undefined. Here we report a discovery lipidomics platform to generate a resource of mass-defined unnamed lipids in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). From a pool of 312 qualified but unknown features, we developed quality metrics to prioritize mass spectrometry signals consistent with genuine undiscovered lipids for chemical identification. Leveraging this list for molecular discovery, we identified a family of lysine lipoamino acids in Mtb that was also broadly conserved among mycobacteria. Identification and disruption of the biosynthetic gene, lysX, attenuated Mycobacterium marinum infection of zebrafish, demonstrating a role in virulence. Recognition and deletion of the orthologous virulence gene, mprF, in Staphylococcus aureus identified the same lipoamino acids. This lipidomic map of mass-defined unknown molecules represents a resource for immediate follow-up in Mtb and established a discovery framework applicable to any bacterial pathogen.

candidates.title: Community-level bisphenol A biotransformation in an activated sludge microcosm.
candidates.abstract: Microbial transformation represents an important pathway for the removal of bisphenol A (BPA), a well-established endocrine-disrupting chemical. However, our understanding of BPA transformation at the community level remains limited. In this study, we established a BPA-degrading activated sludge microcosm, elucidated the BPA transformation pathways with high-resolution mass spectrometry, and characterized the BPA-degrading community with 13C-DNA stable-isotope probing (DNA-SIP), metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, and genome-scale metabolic modeling (GSMM). BPA was transformed primarily via oxidative carbon-skeleton rearrangement, with phenolic-ring hydroxylation and oxidative coupling as minor pathways. Although BPA was rapidly removed, dimeric derivatives persisted throughout the incubation, indicating potential long-term risk. Sphingomonadaceae, Rhizobiaceae, and Comamonadaceae played important roles in BPA biotransformation because they significantly assimilated 13C-BPA and showed increased abundances and activity during the transformation process. Sphingomonadaceae exhibited substantial upregulation of cyp genes putatively involved in initial BPA hydroxylation, and together with Rhizobiaceae and Comamonadaceae, of genes associated with downstream degradation, suggesting potential cooperation among these bacterial guilds. Metatranscriptomics-guided GSMM suggested that abundant non-degrader MAGs may support the community by providing metabolites including carbohydrates, amino acids, and vitamins, whereas BPA degraders shifted from initial metabolite uptake to metabolite secretion during biotransformation.

candidates.title: Cell death and growth dynamics shape DNA-replication-based estimates of microbial growth.
candidates.abstract: A widely used approach for estimating bacterial growth rates is the origin-to-terminus ratio, or peak-to-trough ratio (PTR), which estimates DNA replication activity from origin and terminus copy numbers. Although PTR is theoretically related to bacterial growth rate, it is often compared with, or used to reason about, changes in population size, which reflect the balance between cell division and loss. These quantities may therefore diverge when cell death is appreciable. Here, we used stochastic, cell-based modelling and controlled laboratory experiments to examine how cell death affects the relationship between PTR and changes in population size. We show that transient stress-induced mortality and heterogeneous survival can cause PTR to fail to reflect changes in population size but still reflect bacterial growth rate. We experimentally validated these predictions by exposing Escherichia coli to osmotic shock or antibiotics, and measuring change in population size and DNA replication activity. We further show that initial physiological state, lag before replication resumes, and abrupt growth arrest can alter the relationship between PTR and change in population size. In the presence of mortality, lag can make PTR more reflective of changes in population size whereas it decreases its correspondence with bacterial growth rate. Together, these results demonstrate how cell death and changes in replication dynamics can bias the interpretation of PTR-based estimates of population change under controlled laboratory conditions.

candidates.title: Mitochondrial complex I intermediate assembly factor CIA30 is involved in the senescence and sexual reproduction of Podospora anserina .
candidates.abstract: The conserved CIA30 protein is a critical assembly factor for mitochondrial respiratory complex I. While its dysfunction in eukaryotes is linked to severe respiratory defects and mitochondrial disease, its specific roles in coordinating fungal life history traits, including the balance between aging and reproduction, remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the function of the CIA30 ortholog in Podospora anserina . Deletion of Pacia30 resulted in a striking dual phenotype characterized by a remarkably extended lifespan and severely impaired sexual reproduction, whereas complementation largely restored both traits. The Δ Pacia30 mutant survived beyond 21 days, while sexual development was arrested before ascospore formation. Mechanistically, the mutant exhibited reduced accumulation of reactive oxygen species, accompanied by elevated antioxidant enzyme activities. In addition, the lack of PaCIA30 protein altered mitochondrial respiratory chain composition and was associated with reduced cellular NADH and ATP levels, indicating substantial changes in mitochondrial energy metabolism. Proteomic analysis further revealed extensive metabolic and protein homeostasis remodeling in the mutant. Our findings therefore identify PaCIA30 as a previously unrecognized factor associated with lifespan and sexual development, highlighting mitochondrial complex I assembly as a key link between mitochondrial function, aging, and development in P. anserina . Importance Mitochondrial complex I assembly factors are conserved across eukaryotes, but their impact on life-history traits, such as lifespan and sexual development, remains underexplored. This study reveals that deletion of Pacia30 markedly extends the vegetative lifespan of Podospora anserina while blocking sexual development and preventing the production of mature ascospores. The mutant exhibits reduced ROS accumulation, enhanced antioxidant enzyme activities, and differences in the abundance of proteins associated with energy metabolism, suggesting metabolic adaptation due to the loss of PaCIA30 protein. Our findings establish PaCIA30 as an important determinant of vegetative lifespan and sexual development and highlight the connection between mitochondrial function, redox homeostasis, and fungal development. This work positions P. anserina as a powerful model for dissecting how mitochondrial rewiring can promote longevity at the expense of sexual development, with broader implications for understanding mitochondrial energy reprogramming and aging across eukaryotes.

candidates.title: Implementing microbial source tracking and quantitative microbial risk assessment to characterize fecal pollution and human health risks for recreators in a rural mixed-use watershed.
candidates.abstract: Fecal contamination of surface water poses significant human health risks to recreators and is often influenced by wastewater, agriculture, and wildlife. In this study, we implemented high-throughput sequencing-based microbial source tracking (MST) and quantitative microbial risk assessment (QMRA) to characterize fecal pollution and human health risks in a rural watershed in south-central Texas, USA. Water samples were collected from four sites at 12 time points, and bacterial community composition was characterized using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. Source contributions were estimated with SourceTracker2 by comparing water samples with fecal and wastewater samples. The human-specific Bacteroides marker HF183 was quantified by qPCR and used with literature-reported HF183 and pathogen concentrations in raw sewage and treated wastewater to estimate recreational health risks associated with norovirus, Cryptosporidium spp., Giardia spp., Campylobacter jejuni , Salmonella spp., and E. coli O157:H7. Escherichia coli and HF183 concentrations consistently exceeded the U.S. EPA recreational water quality criteria and recommended risk-based thresholds, with HF183 positively correlated with precipitation. SourceTracker2 indicated that treated wastewater effluent was the dominant known contributor to riverine microbial communities, followed by untreated wastewater, chicken, and cattle feces. QMRA risk estimates varied greatly depending on whether particle aggregation was considered in the norovirus dose-response model. Sensitivity analysis identified swimming ingestion volume, norovirus concentration in treated wastewater, and the norovirus morbidity ratio as key determinants of risk. These findings highlight challenges in MST in rural watersheds, variability in risk across microbial dose-response models, and the need for improved wastewater and stormwater management to mitigate microbial pollution and protect public health. Importance Understanding the sources of microbial pollution in surface waters is essential for protecting public health and guiding effective watershed management. However, identifying pollution sources in rural areas with mixed agricultural, wastewater, and wildlife inputs remains challenging. This study combines next-generation sequencing (NGS)-based microbial source tracking with quantitative microbial risk assessment (QMRA) to link specific contamination sources to human health risks in a rural watershed. By integrating microbial community profiling, source contributions, and health risk modeling, we provide a comprehensive framework to identify dominant contributors, including treated and untreated wastewater, and quantify the associated human health risks. The approach highlights how combining molecular and health risk assessment tools can reveal pollution patterns that conventional monitoring fails to capture. These findings demonstrate the value of NGS-informed monitoring for improving water quality management and mitigating health risks in rural mixed-use watersheds.

candidates.title: A structure-derived contact-network responsiveness atlas of human proteins.
candidates.abstract: Protein structures encode non-local contact organization, but static coordinates do not directly quantify how a contact network responds when effective stabilizing interactions are strengthened or weakened. Here we introduce Contact-Network Responsiveness (CNR), a structure-derived framework that converts residue-level protein coordinates into density-controlled and topology-corrected response descriptors. The method is structure-source agnostic and can be applied to experimentally determined PDB structures, AlphaFold models, or other predicted structures; here, human AlphaFold models serve as the high-coverage structural substrate. Across 22,167 valid human protein models, hydrophobic non-local contact density defined a nearly exact Bethe mean-field baseline for the conformational susceptibility threshold. A graph-aware residue-level extension then revealed systematic graph-dependent deviations from this density-only prediction. We define a topology correction ratio, Rtopo=λfGraph/λfBethe, which provides an operational comparison of the two response models; empirical atlas tails define topology-facilitated, density-dominated and topology-suppressed regimes. CNR descriptors were associated with curated DisProt disorder annotations and broad-coverage UniProt/MobiDB-lite disorder fractions, supporting the interpretation that CNR captures a structural organization axis related to non-local contact availability and responsiveness.

candidates.title: Yoda molecules agonize PIEZO2.
candidates.abstract: Mammalian PIEZO proteins (PIEZO1 and PIEZO2) act as essential mechanosensitive channels. PIEZO1 is thought to be selectively activated by Yoda molecules (Yoda1 and Yoda2). Although a molecular mechanism for PIEZO1 activation by Yoda1 exists, the origin of Yoda1 selective agonism remains obscure. Here, using electrophysiology and calcium imaging in transfected cells, we show that Yoda1 agonizes PIEZO2, but with a distinct efficacy profile compared to PIEZO1. Yoda1 increases single-channel open probability and macroscopic stretch sensitivity of PIEZO2 currents as efficaciously as reported for PIEZO1, but it elicits weak PIEZO2-dependent calcium influx in the absence of external stimulus, an effect detectable only under non-physiological conditions. Yoda1 slows down inactivation of indentation-evoked PIEZO2 currents, but to a lower extent compared to PIEZO1. The Yoda1 analog Dooku1, which does not modulate PIEZO1, slows down PIEZO2 inactivation similarly to Yoda1. Two PIEZO1 agonists unrelated to Yoda1 but thought to populate the same binding site in PIEZO1 have no effect on PIEZO2 inactivation, suggesting that their PIEZO1 selectivity is better than Yoda1. PIEZO2 inactivation is also modulated by Yoda1's more potent analog Yoda2. Using mutagenesis and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that Yoda2's benzoic acid group forms a transient salt-bridge with a conserved arginine in the Yoda binding site (R1724/R2029 in mouse PIEZO1/PIEZO2), explaining the higher potency of this analog for both channels. Together, our study re-evaluates the PIEZO1 selectivity of Yoda molecules and highlights a complex modulatory landscape toward distinct functional properties of PIEZO channels.

candidates.title: Male chickadees with better spatial cognition sire more extra-pair young.
candidates.abstract: Across animal taxa, females commonly mate with more than one male, even in monogamous mating systems. These extra-pair copulations and resulting young may increase the fitness of the female via a variety of mechanisms. The 'good genes' hypothesis suggests that socially monogamous females mate outside their pair bond to increase the fitness of their offspring via indirect genetic benefits, because extra-pair males do not provide parental care. We tested this hypothesis by quantifying extra-pair paternity in nonmigratory, food-caching mountain chickadees ( Poecile gambeli ). Chickadees rely on spatial cognition to recover scattered food caches, and variation in spatial cognition is associated with increased survival, longer lifespan, and is heritable. However, less is known about the role of sexual selection on spatial cognitive abilities. In the current study, we found that (1) males with better spatial cognitive abilities sired more extra-pair young and produced heavier offspring in their own nests compared to their poorer-performing counterparts, and (2) extra-pair males had significantly better spatial cognition than the social males they cuckolded. These results suggest that sexual selection shapes the evolution of spatial cognition in food-caching chickadees and are consistent with the good genes hypothesis, which posits that females gain indirect genetic benefits via extra-pair young.

candidates.title: Deviation from the neutral mutational spectrum in driver genes reveals the distribution of effects of missense oncogenic mutations
candidates.abstract: Although many cancer driver genes have been identified, the full set of variants within these genes that can promote tumorigenesis remains unknown. The contribution of a variant to cancer depends on both its probability of occurrence and the selective advantage it confers. Here, we introduce a metric that quantifies how selection biases the spectrum of observed missense variants in driver genes compared to neutral expectation, and use it to develop a method for estimating the total number of potential driver variants and the distribution of their fitness effects within individual genes. Applying this framework to large cancer cohorts, we estimate that in most oncogenes, nearly all possible missense driver variants have already been observed, whereas in most tumor-suppressor genes, the majority remain undiscovered. These results reveal fundamental differences in how mutation and selection shape nucleotide variation across gene classes and provide a framework for interpreting newly detected variants. Author summary: Which variants spread through Darwinian natural selection depends both on their effects and on how often they arise by mutation. Some point mutations occur much more frequently than others, making them more readily available to selection. Here, we examine how these two factors interact during cancer development. We find that, in genes where many different mutations can promote cancer, the patterns of variants observed in tumors largely reflect their probabilities of arising by mutation. By contrast, in genes where only a few specific mutations can promote cancer, selection strongly favors these variants, even when they are unlikely to arise. Comparing the observed patterns with those expected from mutation alone allows us to infer how selection acts on individual genes during cancer evolution and helps us interpret newly identified variants in these genes.

candidates.title: Assessment of the Production or Protection Benefits of a Maternity Pen in Conserving Endangered Caribou in Northeastern British Columbia, Canada.
candidates.abstract: In British Columbia, Canada, caribou numbers have declined with calf mortality from predation being one proximate cause; an ultimate manifestation of anthropogenic disturbances. Maternity pens directly protect calves from predators, but penning may also improve production of calves because pelleted foods are readily available, highly digestible, and nutrient dense potentially offsetting the energetic cost of previous-year reproduction and increasing current-year calf production. We monitored Klinse-Za caribou in northeastern BC to investigate whether an observed increase in calf recruitment resulted from: protecting calves in a maternity pen, improved calf production due to the pelleted food provided in the pen, or both. We contrasted the potential effects of previous-year reproduction (months with calf-at-heel), current- and previous-year management (penned or not), and cow age in a longitudinal study of vital rates of cows penned or left free-ranging (i.e., not penned). Most (92%) cows were pregnant, with previous-year reproduction and age contributing positive and negative influences on the probability of pregnancy, respectively. Of cows known to be pregnant, 88%-91% had successful parturition and, among penned cows, those retaining a calf-at-heel longer were most likely to have successful subsequent parturition. Overall pregnancy and parturition rates were similar for penned and free-ranging cows. Calf survival was not affected by cow age, previous-year reproduction or previous-year management. Current-year penned calves had a 3.8-fold reduction in risk of mortality compared to calves born outside the pen. Of the penned calves, 11% died mostly from accidents. Of free-ranging calves, 40% died mostly from predation. We concluded that Klinse-za caribou cows were able to maintain their reproductive performance based on natural diets and any additional benefit from ad libitum feeding in the maternity pen was not obvious. The conservation benefit provided by the maternity pen was primarily realized through protection from predators.

candidates.title: Prioritization of Candidate Genes and Predicted Compounds for Presbycusis by Mendelian Randomization With Multidimensional Bioinformatics Analysis.
candidates.abstract: To prioritize candidate genes and computationally predicted compounds for presbycusis, we integrated an exploratory expression screen with two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) using whole-blood eQTL data from the eQTLGen Consortium and presbycusis GWAS data from the EBI database. Functional-enrichment, immune-cell-infiltration, pathway, motif, regulatory-network, and compound-perturbation analyses were performed for biological interpretation. Among 145-gene expression-presbycusis associations evaluated by primary MR, nine associations supported by at least three instrumental SNPs met the nominal IVW threshold of p 0.70 and were selected for exploratory downstream characterization. Immune-infiltration analysis showed higher neutrophil and eosinophil proportions and lower mast-cell and activated dendritic-cell proportions in the older group. GSVA linked GLIPR2 and COL9A2 mainly to WNT/ β -catenin signaling and ESPN and DPP4 to apical-surface signaling. Motif analysis identified cisbp_M6547 as the most enriched motif (NES = 5.31), with predicted enrichment for COL9A2 and ESPN. Expression analysis identified strong correlations between GLIPR2 and CYBA and between ESPN and ACTG1, and a predicted network comprising four mRNAs and 27 miRNAs was constructed. CMap analysis prioritized azacitidine, dilazep, GSK-3 inhibitor II, ivermectin, and sunitinib as compounds with expression profiles inversely correlated with the presbycusis-associated signature. These findings provide genetically informed candidates and testable hypotheses that require independent replication and experimental validation.

candidates.title: A theoretical and simulation-based assessment of the SNP- and haplotype-based genomic prediction in panmictic populations.
candidates.abstract: Background We theoretically and empirically compared single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)- and haplotype-based genomic prediction. We derived and computed the relative prediction accuracy of a quantitative trait loci (QTL) additive value based on two SNPs and a haplotype of size 2 and the relative magnitude of the maximum linkage disequilibrium (LD) values for haplotype and SNP alleles. The empirical assessment was based on two criteria, using a simulated dataset: the efficacy of SNP- and haplotype-based genomic additive relationship matrices to express genotypic similarity for identical by descent (IBD) and identical by state (IBS) alleles, and the additive and epistatic genetic values prediction accuracies over six generations of random matings, assuming seven types of digenic epistasis. Results The values of efficacy of the haplotype-based QTL additive value prediction accuracy, relative to the SNP-based, showed that the two approaches are equivalent. The maximum LD value for a haplotype allele was higher than the maximum LD value for a SNP allele in only 10% of the scenarios. The correlations between the additive and the SNP- and haplotype-based genomic additive matrices showed that haplotypes expressed better than individual SNPs the genotypic similarity for IBD alleles. Considering the efficacy of the SNP- and haplotype-based genomic additive matrices to express genotypic similarity for IBS alleles, the correlations showed that SNPs and short haplotypes are also similar. Considering the additive value prediction accuracy over generations, in the high and low LD populations the increase in the haplotype size from 2 to 10 decreased the prediction accuracy. Regarding haplotypes of size 2, the absolute differences in accuracy between the SNP- and haplotype-based approaches were insignificant. Epistasis had a negative impact on the additive value prediction accuracy. Using SNPs and haplotypes of size 2, the predictions accuracies under epistasis were lower than the accuracies under the additive-dominance model, except for duplicate genes with cumulative effects and non-epistatic gene interaction. The decreases were higher for duplicate epistasis. Conclusions Based on the theoretical and empirical assessments, SNP- and haplotype-based genomic prediction of complex traits are equivalent assuming short haplotypes, regardless of the population LD level, trait heritability, and epistasis type.

candidates.title: Integrating MeSH semantics and knowledge graph topology for structure-agnostic drug-drug interaction prediction.
candidates.abstract: Background Adverse drug-drug interactions (DDIs) cause preventable hospitalizations, but exhaustive experimental screening of all drug pairs is infeasible. Many computational predictors rely on small-molecule structural representations, limiting their direct applicability to biologic therapeutics. We present a structure-agnostic framework that combines semantic representations derived from Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) with graph-derived topology from a Drug-Target-Protein knowledge graph constructed from DrugBank and UniProt. We further examine how MeSH annotation depth is associated with predictive performance. Results In transductive evaluation, latent gated fusion achieved an overall AUROC of 0.988 and improved mean AUROC and F1 over MeSH-only across all six interaction categories. Improvements in AUROC, F1, and precision remained significant after Holm correction for Low-Mid, Mid-Mid, and Mid-Deep interactions, with the largest mean AUROC gain in Low-Mid (+0.0304). In seen-unseen inductive evaluation, each test pair contained one held-out drug and one seen drug, and all DDI edges were excluded from the feature graphs. Fusion achieved an overall AUROC of 0.937, exceeding MeSH-only by 0.045; this improvement remained significant after Holm correction. Mean AUROC gains occurred across all six categories, with recurring improvements in Low-Mid ( + 0.063) and Mid-Mid ( + 0.053) that reached nominal significance, although the inductive category-level evidence remained exploratory. Conclusions MeSH annotation depth is associated with systematic variation in DDI prediction performance that aggregate evaluation can obscure. Recurring gains for Low-Mid and Mid-Mid interactions across evaluation settings support the predictive benefit of combining MeSH semantics with graph-derived topology, with additional transductive evidence for Mid-Deep interactions. The framework provides a common, structure-agnostic representation compatible with both small-molecule and biologic therapeutics and supports first-pass DDI prioritization for subsequent expert assessment. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

candidates.title: Association between duodenal mucosa-associated periodontal bacteria and advanced liver fibrosis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
candidates.abstract: Gut microbiota and periodontal diseases are potential risk factors for duodenal mucosa-associated microbiota in fibrosis progression of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease; however, the specific contribution of duodenal mucosa-associated microbiota remains unclear. Therefore, in this prospective study, we investigated its association with liver stiffness to elucidate its role in disease progression. Duodenal brush samples were collected during endoscopy from patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, classified by liver stiffness measurement into advanced (liver stiffness measurement>8.7 kPa, n = 10) and non-advanced (n = 20) groups. Extracted DNA was subjected to shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Analyses included taxonomy, diversity, differential abundance (edgeR), correlation (Spearman), and receiver operating characteristic predictive modeling, focusing on periodontal bacteria. While microbial diversity did not differ, advanced metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease was characterized by the enrichment of the phylum Pseudomonadota and the genera Haemophilus and Klebsiella. Eight periodontal bacteria, including Campylobacter rectus, Porphyromonas gingivalis, and Fusobacterium nucleatum, were significantly enriched in patients with advanced metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (P < 0.05) and correlated with liver fibrosis markers. A model based on these bacteria discriminated advanced metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease with an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI, 0.634-1.000). Duodenal mucosa-associated microbiota alterations, particularly the enrichment of eight periodontal species, were associated with fibrosis severity. These findings highlight the role of the oral-gut-liver axis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease progression and suggest potential microbial biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

candidates.title: Vascular modelling of peripheral ischaemic disease response.
candidates.abstract: Ischaemic disease presents a significant challenge in medical science due to its widespread manifestations in the body and its tendency to only become overt in its late stages, beyond where current intervention methods are effective. Diseases such as coronary heart disease and peripheral artery disease (PAD) represent leading causes of death and are detrimental to quality of life. Focussing on the latter, PAD incurs an amputation rate of around 25%, largely owing to microvascular disease that prevents tissue recovery even after revascularisation. Current methods for investigating PAD either cannot chart specific vascular determinants, such as with in vivo imaging, or deform and remove subjects from longitudinal studies, such as with ex vivo tissue sampling. Presented to aid live research, computational modelling can collate information and build models of ischaemia using available information and provide a reasonable approximation of the disease's chronology and thus support understanding and advance research of PAD. Proposed here, is a 3D in silico model of ischaemic disease in the limb using a system of purpose-built platforms. Starting with a real micro-computed tomography image of the murine hindlimb, a realistic vessel bed was generated using vascular graphing software, ViGiL. From here, the model was realised in a defined pressure gradient via flow-modelling software, numPTI. With the base model of lower limb arteries, collateral vasculature was generated throughout the vessel space. This provides a bypass system for adaptation post-ischaemia. Upon ischaemic induction, the collateral bed responds to the loss of flow and successfully adapted to recover flow with similar density and distribution of diameters in collateral arterioles (p>> 0.05). Moreover, a satisfactory flow recovery of 50% was achieved after 6 days, showing that the model can reflect the specific vascular environment in which disease is incited. The proceeds of this study lay the groundwork for truly realistic ischaemic models including moving towards a predictive model than can signify when and where key indicators of PAD manifest.

candidates.title: Network pharmacology and bioinformatics analysis of the potential mechanism of morin against myocardial infarction.
candidates.abstract: Background As a typical natural flavonoid compound, morin exerts definite cardioprotective effects. Nevertheless, its specific molecular regulatory mechanisms in the treatment of myocardial infarction have not been fully elucidated. Methods This study combined network pharmacology and bioinformatic strategies to screen candidate targets of morin as well as genes closely associated with myocardial infarction across diverse databases. Further validations were implemented via functional enrichment analysis, three machine learning models including LASSO regression, SVM-RFE and random forest algorithm, immune infiltration assessment and molecular docking verification. Results Through a multi-step screening process, six candidate genes were identified, including ARG1, CDK6, CXCR1, CYP1B1, MMP9, and PFKFB3. These candidate genes are enriched in inflammation- and metabolism-related signaling pathways, including the TNF, AMPK, HIF-1, and IL-17 pathways, as well as pathways involved in arachidonic acid metabolism and phagocytosis. Immune association analysis suggests that these genes are associated with neutrophils, macrophages, and mast cells. Molecular docking simulations predict a potential binding interaction between mulberry pigment and these target proteins. Conclusions Morin may alleviate damage caused by myocardial infarction by regulating immune and inflammatory responses, metabolic processes, and tissue remodeling.

candidates.title: Species diversity increases information flow about predation in bird communities
candidates.abstract: by Agnishikhe Kumar, Jiahao Wu, Ping Ding, Jakob Bro-Jørgensen, Mylène Dutour, Ari E. Martínez, Xingfeng Si, Qiang Zhang, Eben Goodale The Biodiversity-Ecosystem Functioning (BEF) literature has shown species diversity to be essential for ecosystem functioning and services. Yet this concept has not been extended often to behavioral ecology, so that although it is understood that acquiring social information from heterospecific individuals is an important component of ecosystem functioning, it is unclear how animal signaling at the community level, and subsequent information flow, is related to increased species diversity. Eliciting vocal responses using predator models across 10 nature reserves on a latitudinal gradient, we first show that the species diversity of birds is correlated with signaling about predation, both in the low-risk system of mobbing and in the higher-risk system of alarm calls. After finding a similar result across a fragment area gradient in one reserve, we used this system to test how interspecific information flow is affected by species diversity. Potential mechanisms behind this effect include that species are complementary in the characteristics of their mobbing calls, so more species translates into more cumulative information, or there are higher signaling rates as more individuals are involved, or a specific keystone species is more likely to occur. This experiment varied the number of species producing mobbing calls (one, two, four, eight species), with two playback construction methods (standardizing call rate, as typical for BEF experiments, or letting it increase with species richness, as in natural assemblages). Heterospecific mobbing participation (number of vocal species, number of participating individuals), and responses (call rate, probability to call in the first minute and frequency range) increased with species richness. Construction method significantly interacted with species richness, as non-standardized exemplars showed accentuated response as species richness increased. These results match expectations that complementary differences among species in the acoustic characteristics of mobbing calls, and increased call rate, both contribute to the result. There was little evidence that the signals of one particular species changed the experimental result. The overall evidence thus supports the hypothesis that the species diversity of a community is a key component influencing the quantity and the characteristics of signaling and information flow inside it.

candidates.title: When should adaptation arise from a polygenic response versus few large-effect changes?
candidates.abstract: by William R. Milligan, Laura K. Hayward, Guy Sella When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response? There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them. To address this gap, we frame the question in terms of the properties of an adaptive trait. We ask how the genetic basis of adaptation depends on key aspects of genetic variation in the trait and on the degree to which its selection pressures have changed. To this end, we consider a quantitative trait subject to stabilizing selection and model its response when a population at mutation–selection–drift balance experiences a sudden shift in the trait optimum. Using this model, we delimit how the contributions of large-effect and polygenic changes to adaptation depend on the genetics and ecology of adaptive traits, as well as on other salient factors. Thus, we formulate testable predictions for when different modes of adaptation are expected.

candidates.title: Laxative treatment perturbs gut microbiome composition and metabolism in humans independent of short-term fiber consumption: a randomized controlled crossover intervention study.
candidates.abstract: Gastrointestinal transit time is a major ecological determinant of the human gut microbiome, yet causal evidence that disentangles the effects of diet from those of the gut environment remains limited. Here, we conducted a randomized, controlled crossover trial in healthy adults (nine females, four males) consuming fully standardized high-fiber (40 g/d) or low-fiber (10 g/d) diets to assess how manipulating the gut environment using an osmotic laxative (Movicol) affects gut microbial composition and metabolism. Contrary to our hypothesis, laxative treatment did not affect the saccharolytic-to-proteolytic ratio. Yet, it induced a pronounced microbiome perturbation, explaining 16.3% of the variation in microbial community structure, compared with 1.7% explained by diet. The laxative treatment reduced the absolute abundance of several gram-positive commensals, including butyrate-producing taxa, while increasing gram-negative genera such as Bacteroides , Alistipes , and Phocaeicola . Our findings identify perturbations to the gut environment as a prominent short-term driver of human gut microbiome structure, independent of short-term fiber intake. Together, these results challenge a diet-centric view of microbiome modulation and raise concerns about potential detrimental effects on the gut microbiome in chronic use of gut environment-altering drugs such as macrogol-based laxatives.

[Introduction]
The human gastrointestinal tract harbors a dense and diverse microbial community that has co-evolved with its host in a symbiotic relationship. 1 This ecosystem contributes to digestion, host metabolism, and immune regulation, and disruptions to it have been linked to a wide range of diseases and health outcomes. 2 Dietary changes can alter microbial composition within days, and the microbiota can quickly return toward its previous composition after resumption of the habitual diet. 3 Nevertheless, although diet is a key determinant of microbial composition, providing both substrates and selective pressures, 4 interindividual variation in the gut microbiome cannot be fully explained by diet alone. 5 Large cohort studies consistently show that host-derived abiotic factors, particularly gastrointestinal transit time and pH, explain more of the variation in microbiome composition and metabolism between individuals than dietary patterns. 6-11 Observational and in vitro studies have found that a faster colonic transit time is associated with gut ecosystem maturation and a higher ratio of saccharolytic-to-proteolytic fermentation. 12-14 These findings underscore that the gut microbiota is strongly shaped by the physical environment in which it resides. This has led to the proposal of a conceptual framework in which the gastrointestinal environment defines the ecological boundaries within which microbes persist, diversify, and compete, whereas diet shapes the functional niches within those boundaries, primarily through regulating substrate availability. 15 In this context, controlling diet is essential for isolating the effects of environmental drivers such as intestinal transit time by minimizing variation in substrate supply to the gut microbiota.
Transit time can be manipulated with laxatives (which accelerate transit) and antidiarrheals (which slow down transit). Few randomized controlled trials have investigated the direct effects of manipulating gastrointestinal transit on the gut microbiota, 16-19 largely corroborating the findings from observational and in vitro studies. 9 , 11-13 , 20-22 Stephen et al. (1987) demonstrated that senna-induced acceleration of intestinal transit time increased fecal bacterial dry mass. 16 Lewis and Heaton (1997) reported significant changes in WGTT and fecal short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) concentrations following 9-d interventions with wheat bran, senna, and loperamide, separated by washout periods of at least 14 d. 18 Similar

[Materials and methods]
An open, randomized, controlled trial with a parallel whole-meal intervention (low vs. high-fiber diet) and crossover laxative treatment within each arm to manipulate whole-gut transit time (WGTT) in healthy adults was designed (see Figure 1A). The study was conducted at the Department of Nutrition, Exercise, and Sports at the University of Copenhagen, Denmark, from October 2023 to December 2024. The protocol was approved by the ethics committee of the Capital Region of Denmark (H-23033118), and all participants provided written informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and a GDPR consent form, as required by Danish law. The study was registered at Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT06022302) in November 2023. This study followed the SAGER guidelines. Biological sex (female/male) was self‑reported and considered in the study design, including eligibility criteria and stratified randomization. The study was not powered to assess sex‑specific effects; therefore, analyses were not stratified by sex.
Of the 22 enrolled participants, 12 completed the entire study (see full flowchart in Figure 1B). The inclusion criteria were (1) age 18–75 y, (2) BMI 18.5–30 kg/m2, (3) self-reported ≤ 3.5 spontaneous bowel movements per week, (4) willingness to collect and temporarily store biological samples at home, (5) willingness to eat the provided foods, and (6) access to a smartphone. Exclusion criteria were (1) pregnant or lactating women, (2) diagnosis of gastrointestinal (GI) disorders (irritable bowel syndrome, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, inflammatory bowel diseases, gastrointestinal obstruction, ischemic colitis), (3) diagnosis of constipation according to the ROME IV criteria, (4) intake of antibiotics <1 month prior to the intervention or any medication that can affect the outcomes of the study, (5) regular use of diarrhea inhibitors or laxatives, dysphagia, any chronic disease that could affect the outcomes of the study or pose a risk when consuming Movicol, (6) intake of medications potentially altering gastric pH (proton pump inhibitors, histamine receptor antagonists, antacids), (7) intake of medications potentially altering the GIT motility (prokinetics, antiemetic agents, anticholinergic agents, narcotic analgesics, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and peroral glucocorticoids), (8) concurrent participation in another trial, or any condition that lead the project responsible researcher doubt the feasibility of the volunteer's particip

[Results]
We conducted the randomized, controlled, crossover trial in healthy adults (n = 13, Figure 1A) with a self-reported defecation frequency of fewer than 3.5 bowel movements per week from October 2023 to December 2024. Approximately 400 individuals responded to the recruitment ads. Of those, 22 were randomized to the low-fiber (n = 12) and high-fiber (n = 10) diet arms. Four participants in each arm discontinued before the end of the first period due to personal (n = 5) or unrelated medical reasons (n = 3) (Figure 1B). One participant in the low-fiber diet arm discontinued before completing the second period due to an adverse response to the diet and laxative treatment. No serious adverse events occurred during the trial (see Table S7 for details). Consequently, 12 participants completed both crossover periods. In addition, one participant in the high-fiber arm who discontinued before completing the second period, for reasons unrelated to the study, contributed data from the completed period, and was included in relevant available-case analyses. Thus, the available population comprised up to 13 participants (mean age = 46 y, mean BMI = 24.4 kg/m2, mean WGTT = 53 hours; baseline characteristics in Table 1), depending on the outcome and contrast. Testing the low- and high-fiber groups at baseline indicated even alignment of randomization despite the low sample size (Table 1).
Note: Baseline characteristics of participants in the low‑fiber and high‑fiber diet arms. Values are presented as mean (standard deviation) unless otherwise indicated. Hydrogen and methane were measured in breath exhalations in a fasted state. BMI, body mass index; HbA1c, hemoglobin aAc; LDL, low-density lipoprotein; HDL, high-density lipoprotein.
Body weight, physical activity, alcohol and coffee intake appeared stable during the study (Figure S4 and Table S8). The average energy intake was similar across the baseline phases in the low-fiber diet arm; however, in the high-fiber diet arm, it increased during the second baseline phase, concomitant with a rise in average dietary fiber intake (Figure 1C and D). On average, the low-fiber diet halved, and the high-fiber diet doubled the participants' usual intake of dietary fibers (Figure 1D). All meals provided were consumed, except for two individuals on the high-fiber diet who skipped a few entire meals (4%–6% of the meals provided) due to lack of appetite or forgetting to bring them. [Discussion]
Here, we designed a randomized controlled dietary trial with a nested crossover design to examine the causal effects of WGTT and the interaction between diet and WGTT on the microbiome composition and activity. Based on previous observations, 12 , 13 , 17 , 18 , 21 , 63-65 we hypothesized that a faster WGTT would lead to a shift toward more saccharolytic and less proteolytic fermentation. We furthermore hypothesized that the high-fiber diet would similarly promote this shift compared to baseline, whereas the low-fiber diet would do the opposite. The intervention successfully changed stool consistency and frequency, but did not accelerate WGTT as hypothesized. The main outcome of the study was the fecal butyrate-to-urinary p-cresol sulfate ratio, markers of saccharolytic and proteolytic fermentation, respectively, reflecting shifts in microbial fermentative activity. Contrary to our hypothesis, we did not observe an increase in the butyrate/p-cresol-sulfate ratio following laxative treatment. Instead, we observed a tendency toward decreased propionate in both diet arms, along with decreased acetate and a tendency toward decreased butyrate in the high-fiber diet arm when comparing treatment phases. The same trend was observed across most other microbial metabolic activity markers in both diet arms. Although the laxative treatment did not alter WGTT as hypothesized, it imposed ecological stress on the gut microbiome, impacting metabolic efficiency.
The laxative treatment markedly affected gut microbiome composition by significantly reducing the absolute abundance of genera that accounted for 48% of the average relative abundance under the control treatment, corroborating the trend of a reduced metabolic output. Although we did not observe a reduction in total fecal bacterial cell counts following laxative treatment, previous randomized controlled trials that manipulated intestinal transit time with drugs have reported increases in total bacterial mass and total stool weight following laxative treatment 16 , 18-20 . Therefore, our findings appear to differ from those of others. These previous studies all used the laxative medication senna to induce laxative effects. candidates.title: The gut‒kidney axis.
candidates.abstract: Gut-kidney dialog is integral to the holobiont. This review explores the interactions between these two organ-systems across physicochemical, endocrine, immune, and metabolic levels. It is argued that the gut makes physiological concessions favoring the microbiota, which must be assured by the kidneys, extending the concept of renal homeostasis to holostasis . When considering pathological situations, three dimensions of the gut‒kidney axis are identified: (1) the gut causing kidney disease, (2) the effect of renal failure on the gut, and (3) the systemic effects of the gut in renal failure. Causal roles of the gut in enteric hyperoxaluria, IgA nephropathy and diabetic nephropathy are described. The impact of a uremic environment on the gut is discussed. Conversely the intestinal origins of uremic toxins and their impact on distant organs, including the kidneys themselves, are outlined. Special consideration is given to host-microbiota immune interactions, immunosuppressive therapy and kidney transplantation. Therapeutic interventions targeting the gut-kidney axis are appraised.

[Introduction]
The kidneys filter, sort, and drain waste from the holobiont – an ecosystem encompassing the human body and its microbiota. The gut is a vibrant habitat central to the holobiont. Metabolites generated by the microbiota from food in the gut sustain the host, but can also be harmful. Conversely, if host metabolites fail to be eliminated by the kidneys, they overflow into the gut where they can disrupt microbial communities. 1 , 2
In health, by-products of both host and microbial metabolism reach the kidneys via the circulation, where they are eliminated in the urine. The kidneys collaborate with the gut to ensure circulatory homeostasis by regulating salt and water balance. 3 The mucosal immune system is the host’s chief interlocutor with the gut flora, and perturbation of this relationship leads to inflammation that can have consequences both locally and systemically. 4 , 5 As such, the kidneys are susceptible to up-stream processes in the gut, while in turn, a healthy gut depends on the kidneys to prevent stagnation within the holobiont.
Metabolic, cardiovascular and immune-mediated diseases are major causes of kidney failure. Our understanding of how host‒microbiota interactions in the gut contribute to these processes is advancing. 6
In this review, key concepts concerning the gut‒kidney axis are discussed, and interactions between these two organ-systems are explored across three dimensions: (1) the causal role of the gut in kidney disease, (2) the effect of renal failure on the gut, and (3) the systemic effects of the gut in renal failure (Figure 1).

Orange arrow: represents the third dimension, defined by the systemic pathological effects of toxic gut-derived metabolites (uremic toxins) that ordinarily are eliminated by the kidneys, but accumulate in kidney failure; these affect the cardiovascular system, skeleton, erythropoiesis and the kidneys themselves. Over recent decades, we have shifted from viewing the human body through an anthropocentric lens to seeing it as a unique habitat with diverse microbial niches whose inhabitants can influence host health. 58 , 59
The first large, culture-independent insight into the diversity and complexity of the human microbiota was provided by Eckburg et al. in 2005, who analyzed feces and 6 colonic sites across 3 individuals using 16S rRNA sequencing. Differences in microbiota composition were seen to be much greater between individuals than across colonic sites within each individual. 60 Since then, two major groups – the European Metagenomics of the Human Intestinal Tract (MetaHIT) 61 , 62 and the American Human Microbiome Project (HMP) 63–65 – have shone further light on the nature of the human microbiota. The vast majority of microorganisms (>90%) are bacteria, with smaller representation from viruses (5.8%), Archaea (0.8%), and prokaryotes, including yeast and protozoa (0.5%). 62 Among the bacteria, two divisions predominate: Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes. Taxonomic analyses tell us which microbial species are present. Functional analyses define metabolic pathways at play and tell us what the microbial community is doing. While there can be significant variability in the species present at different anatomical niches across populations, core metabolic pathways tend to be preserved. These pathways can either be inferred from 16S rRNA data using bioinformatic tools such as PiCRUSt2, or they can be directly observed using metagenomic analyses. 69

While being impenetrable to pathogens, the gastrointestinal tract must remain permeable to nutrients and permissive to commensals. To achieve this balance, a single layer of epithelium is supported by a diplomatic mucosal immune system which tempers inflammatory responses that would otherwise compromise the mucosal barrier – commensal microorganisms are tolerated, and microaggressions are dealt with passively. The success of this approach lies in an effective physical barrier that pre-empts conflict and by incapacitating potential pathogens until they are eliminated by peristalsis.
The epithelial surface of the gastrointestinal tract is lined with mucins 120 secreted by goblet cells, keeping microorganisms at arms-length from the epithelium. In humans, a single mucus layer in the small intestine extends to become a double-layer in the colon. 120 Mucins are made up of heavily O-glycosylated glycoproteins that form a gel when hydrated, 120 , 121 and serve as an energy source for mucin-degrading members of the microbiota that have adapted to this specific niche. 122 Most innate pattern recognition receptors, such as TLRs, are strategically positioned away from the apical membrane of the intestinal epithelium to avoid false-alarms. 123
Additionally, an arsenal of antimicrobial proteins (AMPs) is secreted along the digestive tract. These AMPs include α-defensins, β-defensins, cathelicidin (LL-37), calprotectins, C-type lectins (RegIIIalpha), lysosyzme C and secretory phospholipase A2 IIa (sPLA2). 124–126
At the cellular level, a tolerant immune response is orchestrated by regulatory T cells (Tregs). 127 Other mechanisms, such as anergy and deletion of antigen-specific effector T-lymphocytes by ILC3 cells, also contribute. 128 Mucosal associated invariant T (MAIT) cells respond to metabolic signals sent by the commensal flora when the microbial community is under threat, by neutralizing invading bacteria and contributing to repair of the mucosal barrier. 129 At a humoral level, the placid nature of immunoglobulin A (IgA) is key, coating bacteria to incapacitate them through “immune exclusion”.

candidates.title: Environmental microbial exposure as an under-measured exposome domain: Links to host microbiomes, immune regulation, and disease epidemiology.
candidates.abstract: Environmental microbial exposure is an under-measured biological component of the exposome and a plausible determinant of immune-mediated disease patterns. Humans encounter microbial communities and products from soil, air, water, vegetation, animals, food systems, farms, indoor dust, healthcare settings, schools, and urban built environments. These exposures may influence gut, skin, airway, oral, and mucosal microbiomes and thereby alter epithelial barrier function, immune tolerance, inflammatory thresholds, and microbial metabolite production. This structured mechanistic narrative review integrates direct environmental-exposure studies, environment-to-host microbiome studies, host-microbiome mechanistic evidence, and translational frameworks. The clearest convergence occurs in asthma and allergic disease, where early-life farm exposure, endotoxin-rich dust, environmental microbial diversity, innate immune modulation, and epithelial A20 regulation support a coherent exposure-response model. Evidence for inflammatory bowel disease and broader respiratory outcomes is biologically credible but less direct, whereas metabolic and systemic inflammatory outcomes remain largely supported by host-microbiome and metabolite mechanisms rather than direct environmental exposure studies. The review therefore distinguishes evidence maturity and mechanistic proximity rather than treating all disease categories equally. It further positions pollution, urbanization, building design, biodiversity loss, diet, antibiotics, and socioeconomic conditions as active modifiers of microbial exposure and host response. Future studies should integrate direct environmental sampling with body-site microbiome profiling, functional multi-omics, immune and barrier biomarkers, geospatial exposure assessment, source tracking, repeated measures, and explicit causal-inference designs. Environmental microbial exposure should be treated neither as uniformly beneficial nor harmful, but as a measurable, context-dependent exposome domain whose health effects depend on composition, dose, timing, route, co-exposures, and host susceptibility.
